title: Practical confinement of general untrusted programs

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a practical execution environment that lets an untrusted program process private information while enforcing limits on where that information can go. Under a stated platform and threat model, ordinary storage and communication paths would be controlled, legitimate outputs would follow the caller’s policy, and covert channels would either be eliminated or have proved leakage bounds. The target includes general mainstream-language programs, supplied binaries and generated code, with enough useful execution and sufficiently low cost for ordinary services.

A covert channel communicates through effects outside the intended output interface, such as changes in execution timing or shared-resource availability. Declaring an output interface is therefore insufficient: enforcement must also account for information visible through the surrounding system. A confinement theorem would state what information release is permitted, through which modeled channels, and under which software and hardware assumptions.

General confinement does not require every program to retain its original behavior or finish successfully. A program that depends on forbidden communication may stop working when confined. The practical ambition is to enforce a general boundary while allowing substantial useful workloads to run within it; preserving every program’s behavior would be a separate and stronger requirement.

significance.text: Lampson distinguished two harms from an untrusted service: performing the wrong computation and leaking the customer’s information without leaving an observable indication. Confinement addresses the second. Achieving the proposed capability at service-scale cost would let organizations entrust data to useful untrusted components with a proved limit on their information release, rather than depending solely on confidence in each component’s implementation.

The direct benefit would be an enforceable information-flow boundary around code that need not itself be trusted. As a conditional downstream possibility, this could make supplied software, plugins and generated code easier to deploy for sensitive processing. Such deployment would still depend on suitable caller policies, useful permitted outputs and acceptable leakage budgets. An allowed output can itself reveal sensitive information if the policy permits it.

Preserving the boundary across multiple components requires more than placing each component in a separate container. Untrusted callees must also be confined, their policies must be compatible, trusted services must satisfy their assumed behavior, and residual leakage must be accounted for across components and repeated executions. Otherwise, individually acceptable channels or leakage allowances could combine into an unacceptable disclosure.

The impact has important limits. A confined program can still compute an incorrect answer. Memory safety alone does not establish confidentiality across all permitted and covert channels, and confidentiality confinement alone does not establish general authorization guarantees or eliminate common implementation vulnerabilities. Its revolutionary contribution would be the practical information-flow guarantee within explicit assumptions, rather than a guarantee of correct or universally secure software.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to be established is general enforcement of caller-controlled information-flow policies, including proved bounds on residual covert leakage, at a cost suitable for ordinary services. The supplied evidence identifies substantial obstacles to this target, but does not establish that every mainstream platform lacks it as of November 1, 2026. The gap described here is the capability whose achievement needs convincing evidence, not a verified field-wide absence claim.

A central barrier is identifying and controlling every relevant information path in a realistic system. Files, persistent state and interprocess communication are only part of the problem. Timing and resource-dependent effects can transmit information even when intended communication interfaces are restricted. Lampson emphasized the difficulty of exhaustive channel identification in systems of moderate complexity; the seL4 assumptions illustrate the distinction between proving confidentiality for modeled storage channels and covering timing behavior.

A second barrier is enforcement cost on shared hardware. Masking resource-dependent behavior or otherwise preventing it from carrying information may be expensive. Allowing bounded leakage can offer an alternative, but a meaningful capacity bound needs a defined leakage metric, observation period, receiver capability and accounting for channels used together. A bound for an isolated channel or execution is insufficient unless its scope matches the intended deployment.

A third barrier is connecting a checked mathematical model to the actual machine. A proof can establish consequences only for modeled behavior and declared assumptions. Hardware behavior, device access and relevant driver behavior therefore need explicit contracts and evidence that those contracts hold. Hardware assistance for timing enforcement could be part of the solution, but a software proof cannot by itself establish every physical assumption on which that assistance depends.

current_state.text: In October 1973, Butler W. Lampson published “A Note on the Confinement Problem” in Communications of the ACM, volume 16, issue 10, pages 613–615. He formulated confinement as preventing a program from communicating information to programs other than its caller and sought enforcement for arbitrary programs, while allowing that some programs would cease to work under confinement. He described enforcement as conceptually straightforward but potentially costly, and discussed bounding covert-channel capacity when the customer accepts some leakage. This establishes the historical goal and its reasoning, rather than a modern implementation result.

The seL4 verification-assumptions page, as characterized in the supplied review, states that its confidentiality proof covers in-kernel storage channels and excludes timing channels. It also explains that the hardware model omits relevant information channels, so the confidentiality conclusion applies only to channels visible in that model. These are meaningful kernel-level guarantees under assumptions; they do not amount to a blanket confinement proof for arbitrary applications running above the kernel.

The same seL4 page assumes that DMA devices are absent or behave appropriately, including not overwriting the kernel. Relevant device and driver behavior requires separate assurance, such as verification or suitable verified wrappers. The readable assumptions page supports these qualifications. The supplied review found the saved FAQ copy unreadable, so that copy provides no additional assessable support; its limitation does not invalidate the readable assumptions page.

Another supplied artifact was identified by the review as the seL4 Reference Manual, version 17.0.0, dated October 30, 2026, rather than a PDF reproduction of the assumptions page. Its extracted introduction describes kernel functional-correctness proofs across multiple architectures and platforms, with security-proof coverage depending on the platform. The extraction was truncated and reported problems, including pages without extractable text. It therefore supports limited statements about kernel-proof scope, not comprehensive manual coverage or a new whole-system confinement result.

The research attributed a CHERI/Morello study to Xiaoyang Sun, Jeremy Singer and Zheng Wang at IISWC 2025, with DOI 10.1109/IISWC66894.2025.00042, and described capability-based memory-safety experiments with overhead ranging from small amounts to approximately 1.65× depending on workload and ABI. The supplied review found only a generic site label in the saved IEEE page, with no substantive article text. Consequently, that copy does not verify the article identity, experimental platform, workload scope, interpretation of the performance ratio or numerical range. The figure remains an unverified research-note claim, not an established measurement in this record; the extraction limitation is not evidence that the study or result is false.

The supplied freshness record is empty. Neither the historical formulation nor the documented limitations of a particular seL4 proof establish whether a mainstream platform meets the full proposed target as of November 1, 2026. Present-day availability, deployment breadth and ordinary-service cost therefore remain unresolved on this evidence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed feasibility demonstration: run a database engine, build system or document renderer on a shared machine under a published platform description, threat model and caller-controlled channel policy. Specify protected information, authorized outputs, attacker access, receiver capabilities and the relevant storage, interprocess communication, file and timing paths. State which program behaviors may be blocked and which useful operations the demonstration must preserve.
completion_criteria.label: Database, build, or renderer confined under published caller channel policy

completion_criteria.text: Proposed leakage criterion: before testing, register the leakage metric, observation interval and permitted aggregate bound. Machine-check the enforcement argument and relevant channel bounds against the system model, including how bounds compose across channels and repeated activity. Separately justify the modeled channel inventory and document the connection between the model, implementation and hardware. A checked proof would establish its conclusion under those assumptions; it would not by itself prove that the model captures every physical information path.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered aggregate leakage bound machine-checked with channel composition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed adversarial evaluation: give a red team the binary and chosen-input access, plant a secret, and have the team attempt disclosure through the specified channels. Make attack procedures and observations reproducible within the declared threat model. Failure to exceed the bound would provide experimental evidence alongside the proof, rather than prove a universal capacity bound through unsuccessful attacks.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible red-team attempts to disclose planted secret through specified channels

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance criterion: on a stated workload, require confined throughput to reach at least half the unconfined baseline under comparable resource allocations. This is a chosen feasibility threshold, not an established standard. Publish the workload, baseline, configurations and measurement method so others can reproduce the comparison. Hardware-dependent timing enforcement is acceptable if its contract, proof assumptions and independent validation are explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Confined throughput at least half unconfined baseline under comparable resources

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility criterion: release enough implementation, proof and configuration material for independent reproduction, and evaluate materially different workloads and allowed program interactions. A single application would demonstrate feasibility within its stated boundaries. A finite suite would establish demonstrated breadth; arbitrary-program coverage would require a general enforcement argument specifying the supported execution model, restrictions and treatment of programs that cannot complete under confinement.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction across materially different workloads and allowed interactions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: SWE-01, “Push-button verifying compilation for practical systems,” and SWE-02, “Certified synthesis of system-scale programs from reviewable specifications,” concern routes to obtaining programs with guarantees. SWE-07 concerns enforcing an information-flow boundary around code that may remain untrusted or functionally incorrect. Verification or synthesis could support a confinement implementation, but the roster titles do not establish their detailed guarantees or make either a prerequisite for confinement.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-03, “Demonstrable adequacy of a specification against intent and the environment,” overlaps with the need to show that a confinement policy and threat model capture the intended privacy boundary and relevant environment. SWE-05, “Assurance that stays proportional to each behavioral change,” concerns maintaining assurance as systems evolve. SWE-07 supplies a particular security property whose model, channel inventory and proof assumptions would need that ongoing care.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-04, “A compositional calculus for concurrent systems that fail,” and SWE-10, “Proof-carrying behavioral composition across trust boundaries,” overlap with reasoning about interacting components. SWE-07 specifically requires compatible information-flow policies, confinement of untrusted callees and aggregate leakage accounting. Neither general behavioral composition nor reasoning about concurrent failures automatically establishes those confidentiality properties.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-06, “Sound behavioral recovery of legacy systems,” could help characterize existing software before confinement, while SWE-11, “Proved semantics-preserving transformation of practical systems,” concerns transformations that retain program meaning. SWE-07 can impose restrictions that change observable behavior or prevent completion. It therefore remains distinct from recovering behavior or preserving all original semantics.

Roster-based synthesis: SWE-08, “Sequential meaning for fault-tolerant distributed execution,” and SWE-09, “Observable determinism as the default for parallel systems code,” concern execution semantics. Confinement concerns which information an observer may learn. Predictable logical results do not by themselves establish confidentiality of timing or resource use, while a confined program need not have deterministic or sequential behavior.

Operating-system isolation, capability security, formal verification and information-flow control are closely related foundations. Memory safety restricts invalid memory access; confinement additionally concerns disclosure through allowed interfaces and covert effects. seL4 illustrates how strong formal guarantees can have explicitly bounded channel coverage. The unverified CHERI/Morello study cannot establish achieved confinement or performance in this record.

change_log.change: Clarified that arbitrary-program confinement can block behavior or prevent completion.
change_log.reason: The reviewed Lampson text does not require every confined program to continue working.

change_log.reason: The empty freshness record and source-specific limitations do not establish field-wide unavailability as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Qualified compositional benefits with compatible policies, trusted-service assumptions, confinement of callees and aggregate leakage accounting.
change_log.reason: Separate component boundaries do not automatically compose into an end-to-end confidentiality guarantee.

change_log.change: Separated confidentiality from functional correctness, general authorization, memory safety and broad vulnerability elimination.
change_log.reason: The original significance text implied guarantees beyond those established by confinement.

change_log.change: Retained the seL4 storage-channel result, timing exclusion and DMA assumptions, and distinguished kernel proofs from arbitrary-application guarantees.
change_log.reason: These are supported achievements and limitations whose scope matters to the concept.

change_log.reason: Saved-source metadata does not eliminate the access and extraction limitations reported by the review.

change_log.reason: The quantitative claim remains unresolved; lack of substantive article text does not show that it is false.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration with leakage definitions, proof-to-hardware obligations, reproducibility and generality boundaries.

unresolved_issues: Whether any mainstream platform meets the complete confinement target as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The attributed IISWC 2025 CHERI/Morello study’s identity, experimental scope, ABI-dependent results and approximately 1.65× performance figure require substantive article evidence.
The saved seL4 FAQ was unreadable in the supplied review; the manual extraction was truncated and incomplete. Neither supports conclusions beyond the scope described here.
No specific target platform, supported program model, channel inventory, leakage metric, observation interval, receiver model or aggregate leakage budget has been selected.
The practical cost of enforcing the full proposed boundary across useful workloads, and the hardware assumptions needed to do so, remain to be demonstrated.
The other roster entries have titles but no supplied definitions or evidence; their relationships are conceptual synthesis rather than validated dependency claims.

The review recommended removing the unverifiable numerical performance result from the current-state account. Its rejection as an established result is adopted, but the number is retained as an explicitly unresolved research attribution to preserve quantitative detail without inventing a resolution.

brief.title: Running untrusted software with limits on data leaks
possible: You could let software you do not trust process private information while enforcing your rules about what it may reveal. This would cover supplied programs, plugins and generated code, at a cost ordinary services could afford.

The boundary would cover files and messages as well as covert channels: hidden ways to communicate through timing or shared computer resources. Such channels would be blocked or have a proved limit on how much information they could carry.
why: Organizations could use useful software for sensitive work without relying solely on trust in its authors. The protection would come from an enforced boundary around the running program.
This could make supplied software and generated code easier to deploy wherever private information needs processing.

sources.showed: The FAQ explains practical implications of devices that can access memory directly.
sources.cited_for: Device behavior matters to the security assumptions of the operating system.
sources.not_established: Device guidance does not establish a complete boundary against information leaks from general programs.

sources.showed: The seL4 kernel, the core of an operating system, has a confidentiality proof covering its internal storage channels. The proof excludes timing channels and depends on hardware assumptions.
sources.quote:
As mentioned above, in practice the proof covers all
    in-kernel storage channels but does not cover timing channels
sources.cited_for: Mathematical guarantees can cover specific information paths while leaving others outside their scope.
sources.not_established: The proof does not establish confinement of general applications across timing channels and the surrounding system.

sources.who: Butler W. Lampson, Xerox Palo Alto Research Center
sources.showed: Lampson demonstrated how a service could leak information through files and shared resources. He proposed rules for confinement and discussed limiting hidden communication when blocking it costs too much.
sources.quote:
Using these procedures and three files called data, sendclock, and receiveclock, a service
can send a stream of bits to another concurrently running program.
sources.cited_for: Preventing leaks requires controlling hidden communication as well as ordinary outputs.
sources.not_established: The conceptual rules do not demonstrate a practical system for general programs at ordinary-service cost.

sources.who: Xiaoyang Sun, Jeremy Singer and Zheng Wang
sources.showed: The work is described as an experimental study of CHERI/Morello memory safety, which restricts invalid memory access, and its performance cost.
sources.cited_for: The study concerns the cost of memory protection.
sources.not_established: Memory safety alone does not establish control over all ways private information can escape.

shown: The seL4 project has proved confidentiality for storage channels inside an operating-system kernel. That is a concrete guarantee within a defined model, but it leaves timing channels outside the proof.

Lampson laid out why even apparently harmless access to files or shared resources can let secrets escape. His proposed rules explain the challenge; they do not demonstrate the full practical capability.
missing: A useful general-program demonstration must enforce the caller’s disclosure rules across ordinary and hidden communication paths.
A checked proof must bound total leakage across channels, cooperating components and repeated runs.
The mathematical model must be connected to actual hardware, devices and the software controlling them.
Independent experiments must demonstrate useful performance across different workloads.

milestones.label: A useful application runs under explicit disclosure rules
milestones.explanation: A database, build system or document renderer would have to run on shared hardware under published disclosure rules and attacker assumptions. This would demonstrate useful work within a defined boundary.

milestones.label: A checked proof bounds total information leakage
milestones.explanation: A computer-checked proof would have to meet a leakage limit declared before testing, combining channels and repeated activity under justified machine assumptions. This would give the boundary a precise mathematical meaning.

milestones.label: Reproducible attacks test the leakage limit
milestones.explanation: An attack team would have to try to disclose a planted secret through the specified channels using reproducible procedures. This would test the system alongside the proof without turning unsuccessful attacks into a universal guarantee.

milestones.label: Protected execution retains at least half the throughput
milestones.explanation: The protected workload would have to complete work at least half as fast as its unprotected baseline with comparable resources. This would meet the proposed threshold for practical performance.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results across different workloads
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results across materially different workloads and permitted interactions. This would establish demonstrated breadth, while general coverage would still require an argument covering supported programs.

uncertain: Whether any mainstream platform already meets the complete target remains unresolved.
The supported programs, attacker capabilities, observation period and acceptable total leakage still need to be chosen.
The cost of controlling hidden communication across useful workloads, and the hardware assumptions required, remain open.

page.title: Confinement of untrusted programs
page.definition: A caller can give confidential data to an untrusted program and receive its result. The execution environment prevents the program from disclosing information to anyone the policy does not authorise. Under its stated hardware and software assumptions, the guarantee covers both storage channels, where another program can read a change in shared state, and timing channels, where another program can observe a change in how long an operation takes.

goal.need: A browser needs to know which sites its user visits. Of 424 Android browsers studied, 37 shared browsing history for which investigators could identify no feature requiring disclosure. Confinement would let people give third-party software the data it needs and still control who may learn it. Memory permissions alone cannot provide that control. Even programs with separate memory can communicate through changes in execution time, so the guarantee depends on hardware that lets the operating system isolate those timing effects.

figures.caption: Measured shared-kernel timing channel on x86 in the 2019 seL4 experiment.
figures.note: Mutual information estimates information revealed per input symbol. The protected measurement is below the tool's approximately 0.001-bit resolution; it does not establish zero capacity.

statements.body: Xerox Palo Alto Research Center, Butler W. Lampson
statements.quote: We want to be able to confine an arbitrary program.
statements.context: Lampson's research formulation permits confinement to stop programs whose behaviour requires forbidden communication.

statements.body: UNSW Sydney Trustworthy Systems, seL4 developer
statements.quote: Design, implementation, evaluation and verification of black-box OS abstractions and mechanisms for time protection: the prevention of timing channels.

statements.body: PISTIs-V project, UNSW Sydney Trustworthy Systems
statements.quote: It aims to develop a reference system with proofs of strong safety and security properties covering hardware and software and their interaction.
statements.context: PISTIs-V is funded through the German Cyberagentur's ÖvIT programme and targets embedded and cyber-physical systems.

statements.body: German Cyberagentur, ÖvIT programme, PISTIs-V project description
statements.quote: Dadurch werden keine geschützten Informationen preisgegeben, auch nicht durch mikroarchitektonische Timing-Kanäle.
statements.context: The programme calls for proof that LionsOS confines untrusted components even when processor timing is observable. It gives the project term as September 2024 to September 2027.

completion.title: A reference system proves confinement of untrusted programs, including microarchitectural timing channels.
completion.criterion: On the embedded LionsOS reference system, prove that untrusted programs cannot disclose information contrary to the system's policy, including through microarchitectural timing channels. Establish the claim for the implemented OS and its embedded-system services under explicit hardware and software assumptions. Verify critical drivers against the verified hardware of the devices they control, and verify the fence.t processor mechanism used for time protection on CVA6 RISC-V. The policy defines which releases are allowed.
completion.set_by: German Cyberagentur, ÖvIT programme, PISTIs-V project description; detailed project goals published by UNSW Trustworthy Systems. The published target concerns a LionsOS/RISC-V embedded reference system.
completion.threshold_quote: Die verifizierten Eigenschaften von LionsOS beinhalten den Beweis, dass nicht vertrauenswürdige Komponenten eingeschränkt werden. Dadurch werden keine geschützten Informationen preisgegeben, auch nicht durch mikroarchitektonische Timing-Kanäle.
completion.basis: PISTIs-V joins confinement, timing-channel prevention and verified hardware/software integration in an operating-system reference system. This supplies an external test for the core capability. Its scope is embedded systems; it defines no general-program workload suite, acceptable slowdown or nonzero leakage allowance. Lampson supplies the general confinement formulation; NIST leaves permitted channel bandwidths to each organisation.

milestones.title: A machine-checked proof establishes nonleakage for a kernel's C implementation.
milestones.criterion: Prove that each partition's observations depend only on authorised sources and the scheduler. Start from a configured kernel state satisfying the invariants, a consistent and well-formed access policy, the safety condition on cross-partition capabilities, and the timer-only interrupt restriction. The theorem covers storage channels and logical time and assumes correct compilation, assembly, hardware and boot code.
milestones.set_by: Information-flow verification convention: a machine-checked noninterference theorem. The specific test is Murray and colleagues' 2013 seL4 Theorem 2, published for the stated seL4 configuration.
milestones.threshold_quote: Theorem 2: seL4’s C implementation enforces information flow security.

milestones.title: One channel measures below 1 millibit per input or within the 95% zero-leakage bound.
milestones.criterion: For one specified channel and configuration, estimate mutual information M in bits per input. Record M < 0.001 bit as below the tool's resolution. Otherwise shuffle the association between inputs and outputs 100 times and use the shuffled estimates to calculate M₀, the upper 95% bound under zero leakage. Record M ≤ M₀ as consistent with zero leakage. Both conclusions apply only to the tested channel and dataset.
milestones.set_by: Ge and colleagues, published experimental protocol in Time Protection: The Missing OS Abstraction, Sections 5.1 and 5.3. The detection criterion belongs to this experiment.
milestones.threshold_quote: others are consistent with no channel or below the 1 mb tool resolution.

milestones.title: An OS model enforces confidentiality for every observing domain, including its observations of time.
milestones.criterion: Machine-check observer-relative confidentiality for every user domain in a generic OS model. Include observable time, partitioned and resettable processor state, interrupts and the communication that the policy permits. Under the model's hardware and OS assumptions, each domain's observations may depend on another domain's data only through the specified policy channels.
milestones.set_by: Formal-verification convention: a machine-checked security theorem. The specific property is Sison and colleagues' observer-relative confidentiality definition and Theorem 1, peer reviewed at FM 2023.
milestones.threshold_quote: Theorem 1 (OS model enforces confidentiality with time protection).

milestones.title: A kernel's C implementation proves time protection, including permitted cross-domain communication.
milestones.criterion: Complete the developer's roadmap tasks 2B and 2C, carrying time protection through refinement to C code, and task 2D, preserving it across permitted cross-domain communication. Retain the stated hardware contract. Sison's seL4 Summit 2026 abstract reports implementation and evaluation of shared-memory and notification mechanisms and describes their formal verification as continuing work. The conference talk is not a peer-reviewed implementation proof.
milestones.set_by: UNSW Trustworthy Systems, seL4 verification roadmap tasks 2B–2D, published in 2024; time-protection verification is an activity of the government-funded PISTIs-V project.

milestones.title: Device hardware refines the formal interface used to verify its driver.
milestones.criterion: Prove that a device implementation refines its formal interface model, then verify its driver against that interface. This combines PISTIs-V's driver/hardware objective with its published device-refinement test. Murphy and colleagues' 2025 paper demonstrates the specification approach on one I2C controller. Tyler and colleagues' 2026 paper verifies one Pancake Ethernet driver under encoded device and OS interfaces. These establish separate component results.
milestones.set_by: PISTIs-V project goals 2–3 and UNSW Trustworthy Systems' Formalisation of Device Interfaces project, Solution section.

milestones.title: Composing OS-service proofs establishes a system-wide information-flow property.
milestones.criterion: State an information-flow policy for the assembled OS. From local proofs for its services and the protocols through which they communicate, derive that the services running together enforce the policy. State the kernel and hardware guarantees on which the derivation depends.
milestones.set_by: UNSW Trustworthy Systems, Compositional Proof Methods project Aim and verification roadmap task 1E; a PISTIs-V activity published for component-based OSes including LionsOS.
milestones.threshold_quote: Scalable verification of global safety and security guarantees for component-based OSes by composing local per-component proof efforts.

milestones.title: A confined procedure can return a result but cannot write through its inherited object references.
milestones.criterion: Invoke a procedure with a caller-supplied input and an authorised output. Remove modification rights from every object reference inherited from the procedure and preserve that restriction on calls made through inherited procedure references. References passed explicitly by the caller retain their granted rights. The test covers writes through object references.
milestones.set_by: Cohen and Jefferson, Hydra confined-call semantics, section 3.5 of Protection in the Hydra Operating System.
milestones.threshold_quote: only the inherited capabilities and not those passed as arguments have MDFYRTS removed.

milestones.title: seL4's abstract specification bounds the addresses touched on behalf of each security domain.
milestones.criterion: In seL4's abstract kernel specification, prove that the addresses touched on behalf of a domain form a subset of the addresses its security policy allows. Establish the kernel invariants, access-control properties and information-flow properties needed for that argument.
milestones.set_by: UNSW Trustworthy Systems, seL4 time-protection verification roadmap, task 2A.
milestones.threshold_quote: TA ⊆ domain’s addresses (according to security policy)

milestones.title: A proof establishes that CVA6's fence.t instruction enforces its timing-isolation contract.
milestones.criterion: Formally verify the CVA6 hardware implementation of fence.t against the contract used by the OS. Establish that it clears the on-core microarchitectural state covered by the contract and that the time to switch domains is independent of the preceding domain's execution history.
milestones.set_by: German Cyberagentur, ÖvIT programme, PISTIs-V processor-verification objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: verify other critical hardware components, including the fence.t instruction

milestones.title: A refinement proof establishes time protection for seL4's C implementation.
milestones.criterion: Carry the time-protection property of seL4's abstract specification through its executable specification to its C implementation. Account for the addresses touched at each level and prove that the implementation preserves the required isolation under the stated hardware contract.
milestones.set_by: UNSW Trustworthy Systems, seL4 time-protection verification roadmap, tasks 2B and 2C.

milestones.title: Verified seL4 communication mechanisms preserve time protection across security domains.
milestones.criterion: Implement permitted communication between domains and prove that it preserves time protection. For a one-way communication mechanism, establish that only the specified information can flow forwards and that timing reveals no additional information in either direction.
milestones.set_by: UNSW Trustworthy Systems, seL4 time-protection verification roadmap, task 2D.
milestones.threshold_quote: 2D Implement and verify for cross-domain communications

milestones.title: A device implementation provably refines its formal interface specification.
milestones.criterion: Give a formal specification of the device behaviour visible to software and prove that every such behaviour of the hardware implementation is allowed by the specification.
milestones.set_by: UNSW Trustworthy Systems, Formalisation of Device Interfaces project within PISTIs-V.

milestones.title: A device driver is proved correct against its specified hardware and OS interfaces.
milestones.criterion: State the behaviour assumed of the device and the obligations imposed by the OS interface. Prove that the driver implementation operates correctly under those assumptions and meets those obligations for all behaviours admitted by the interfaces.
milestones.set_by: PISTIs-V, project goal 2 on correct operation of device drivers.
milestones.threshold_quote: verifying device drivers for correct operation and interfacing to the hardware

not_found: No external general-workload slowdown limit or universal aggregate covert-leakage budget was found in the standards, programme descriptions and prize searches.
No completed published hardware/software confinement proof meeting the integrated PISTIs-V target was located.

results.finding: seL4: machine-checked nonleakage proof applies to 8,830 lines of C code.
results.detail: The theorem assumes initial invariants, a consistent well-formed policy, safe cross-partition capabilities and only timer interrupts, as well as correct compiler, assembly, hardware and boot code. It covers storage channels and logical time; fine-grained hardware timing is outside the model. The text does not establish peer review.
results.quote:
Theorem 2: seL4’s C implementation enforces infor-
mation ﬂow security.

results.finding: One I2C controller’s address-decoding submodule was proved behaviorally equivalent to its specification.
results.detail: The proof for the controller’s core was still in progress, and driver verification was a future goal. The source is an ACM workshop paper; the supplied text does not establish peer review.
results.quote:
For the i2c_reg_top submodule, we have completed all the
three steps of Section 3.1, resulting in a proof of behavioural
equivalence between the spec and the original Verilog design.

results.finding: One Ethernet driver was verified against encoded device and OS interfaces.
results.detail: The device protocol was translated from the hardware manual. The paper does not prove that the device implementation refines the interface used to verify the driver.
results.quote:
We verify two LionsOS components: the NIC driver and
the library implementing the SPSC queues (Section 3.1). We
prove all properties discussed in Section 3.3, without assum-
ing that the driver executes on the same core as the rest of
the OS, i.e. the system is multicore-safe.

results.finding: Experimental seL4 on CVA6: MICRORESET closed tested timing channels across configurations, using 1 million repeated attacks per measurement.
results.detail: This is an empirical result on an unverified experimental kernel. It does not prove time protection through refinement to C or preservation across permitted cross-domain communication. Cross-core leakage was outside the study.
results.quote:
The channel is consistently closed across conﬁgu-
ration and attacks, as supported by Table 1.

results.finding: Theorem 1 proves information-flow security for the seL4 abstract specification.
results.detail: The model permits specified inter-partition communication and exposes time coarsely through interrupts, but does not model the microarchitectural state required for time protection.
results.quote:
Theorem 1: seL4’s abstract speciﬁcation enforces in-
formation ﬂow security.

results.finding: Theorem 2 establishes information-flow security for seL4’s C implementation.
results.detail: The proof permits restricted cross-partition communication and covers storage channels and logical time. It does not establish time protection: fine-grained hardware timing and covert timing channels remain outside the proof.
results.quote:
Theorem 2: seL4’s C implementation enforces infor-
mation ﬂow security.

results.finding: seL4 time-protection evaluation: 255,040 observations yielded 0.6 millibits of measured leakage in the protected kernel-channel test.
results.detail: The paper implements and evaluates time-protection mechanisms, including an inter-domain IPC benchmark, but does not prove refinement to C or preservation across permitted communication. It reports a residual L2 channel on x86.
results.quote:
The bottom graph is with full time protection,M =
0.6 mb,M0 = 0.1 mb, n = 255, 040 (1 mb = 10−3 bits).

results.finding: A generic OS time-protection model is machine-checked, with an example instantiation for 2 system calls.
results.detail: The proof permits policy-authorised communication under an explicit hardware/software model, but does not refine a kernel implementation to C or verify its cross-domain communication mechanisms.
results.quote: This includes an instantiation of our generic model, for a pair of system calls with tightly speciﬁed policy channels, to ensure it is nontrivial.

results.finding: For the seL4 kernel's C implementation, an Isabelle/HOL-checked confidentiality proof covers all in-kernel storage channels.
results.detail: For supported architectures and compiler settings, the page also reports verification of compiler and linker output. This leaves the milestone's logical-time requirement unverified by this source.
results.quote:
in practice the proof covers all
    in-kernel storage channels but does not cover timing channels

results.finding: CVA6 branch history table with write-through L1 and MICRORESET, 1 million trials, 0.0 millibit per input.
results.detail: The paper's separate zero-leakage analysis uses 1,000 random pairings. The direct threshold is sufficient for this result.

results.finding: CVA6 fence.t with padding, 1 million trials, 1.4 millibits per input in the write-back L1 context-switch channel.
results.detail: The write-back experiment used a 22,000-cycle pad from the timer interrupt. The measurement supports consistency with zero leakage for that dataset.

results.finding: OpenC910 L1I with fence.t.s measured 3.2 millibits, within its reported zero-leakage bound. Sample size unspecified.
results.detail: The comparison applies to the tested channels and datasets. The supplied manuscript gives no publication venue or review status.

results.finding: For one LionsOS Ethernet driver, Viper verifies four correctness properties against the specified hardware and OS interfaces.
results.detail: The proof trusts the Pancake-to-Viper transpiler and the manually encoded weak-memory model. The hardware contract comes from the device manual. The source is an ACM workshop proceedings paper.
results.quote:
The combination of these four properties establish the
driver’s safety and correctness

results.finding: Haswell seL4 timer-interrupt channel with IRQ partitioning (n = 11,029) measured 0.5 millibit per input.
results.detail: The text identifies the definitive publication as a EuroSys 2019 conference paper. The schema has no conference category, so the author version is classified as a report.
results.quote:
IRQ partitioning results in an
uninterrupted time slice for the spy, and a closed channel
(M = 0.5 mb,M0 = 0.7 mb, n = 11, 029).

results.finding: Isabelle/HOL proves observer-relative confidentiality for every user domain in 1 generic OS model.
results.detail: The model assumes partitioned memory and interrupts, resettable processor state, deterministic scheduling, bounded operation latencies and padding to a predetermined switch completion time.
results.quote:
Formally, we then prove that Deﬁnition 1 holds
at all times as seen by every possible user domain:
Theorem 1 (OS model enforces conﬁdentiality with time protection).
∀u. obs-conﬁdentiality u

results.finding: Isabelle/HOL verifies the generic OS model's time-protection obligations for 2 one-way messaging system calls.
results.detail: The example models capability-based authorisation and permits disclosure to the recipient only when the call is authorised. Its proof applies at the generic OS model level.
results.quote:
We provide an example instantiation of the parameters that we prove meets
these obligations: a simple model of capability-based access control over a broad-
cast/subscribe pair of system calls for one-way messaging between domains.

results.finding: Proofcraft reports a completed seL4 implementation confidentiality proof for one architecture, AArch64.
results.detail: The announcement refers readers elsewhere for the assumptions and mentions Isabelle/HOL for seL4 verification generally. The supplied text does not identify the machine-checked statement for this result.
results.quote:
Thanks to continued support from
NCSC
, this milestone completes the formal
proof that the seL4 implementation code on AArch64 enforces security isolation
of the applications running on top (under the assumptions listed
here
).

results.finding: Isabelle/HOL Theorem 4.2 proves conditional confidentiality for a generic time-protection extension that includes observable wall-clock time.
results.detail: The model assumes hardware-enforced partitioning, correct resets and worst-case padding on a single core without hardware multithreading.
results.quote: For all kernel models that meet these requirements, the above claims are formally verified in Isabelle/HOL.

results.finding: seL4's abstract specification tracks touched addresses for user-controlled objects, with the required subset bound stated in Proposition 4.1.
results.detail: Abstract tracking covers user-controlled kernel objects. Kernel globals receive concrete addresses at lower refinement levels, and the no-fail proofs needed to establish coverage of actual accesses remain unfinished.
results.quote:
We therefore add it as a
ghost state
field
in the seL4 abstract specification – that is, state that is intended to assist
proofs but that should not impact the functional semantics of the actual system.

results.finding: Isabelle/HOL proves nonleakage for one seL4 kernel implementation spanning 8,830 lines of C.
results.detail: Logical time is represented by the interrupt oracle. Fine-grained timing effects such as cache leakage and timeslice overruns are outside the theorem.
results.quote:
Theorem 2: seL4’s C implementation enforces infor-
mation ﬂow security.

results.finding: Isabelle/HOL proves partition-relative confidentiality in one 4,970-line seL4 abstract kernel model.
results.detail: Only timer interrupts are enabled. The proof treats the global schedule and logical time as observable and excludes fine-grained processor timing.
results.quote:
Theorem 1: seL4’s abstract speciﬁcation enforces in-
formation ﬂow security.

results.finding: seL4’s nonleakage proof excludes storage back-channels for two mechanisms used for one-way communication.
results.detail: Inert copies of cross-partition capabilities keep channel destruction from signalling in both directions. Shared-cache timing and timeslice overruns remain outside the guarantee.
results.quote:
The information
ﬂow security theorem implies that these primitives are free of
storage back-channels, and that the dynamic intra-partition
services do not violate information ﬂow security either.

results.finding: Haswell seL4 timer-interrupt channel with IRQ partitioning, 11,029 samples, 0.5 millibits per input.
results.detail: The supplied text is the author’s version of a peer-reviewed EuroSys proceedings paper. The available kind labels lack a conference option, so report is used. The journal-specific peer_reviewed flag is false.
results.quote:
IRQ partitioning results in an
uninterrupted time slice for the spy, and a closed channel
(M = 0.5 mb,M0 = 0.7 mb, n = 11, 029).

results.finding: One generic OS model has an Isabelle/HOL confidentiality theorem covering every user domain, including its observations of time.
results.detail: The model assumes deterministic scheduling, partitioned memory and devices, interrupt masking, and bounded interrupt handling and flushes. Domain switches reset flushable state, flush shared cache state, and pad to a predetermined time. System-call handlers must satisfy the stated policy obligations.
results.quote:
Theorem 1 (OS model enforces conﬁdentiality with time protection).
∀u. obs-conﬁdentiality u

results.finding: Two modelled system calls, broadcast and subscribe, satisfy machine-checked policy obligations for one-way messaging between domains.
results.detail: The proof covers an instance of the generic OS model with capability-based authorisation and tightly specified policy channels.
results.quote:
This includes an instantiation of our generic model, for a pair of system calls
with tightly speciﬁed policy channels, to ensure it is nontrivial.

results.finding: Cheshire I2C has a formal interface specification and behavioural equivalence to the original Verilog for 1 submodule, i2c_reg_top.
results.detail: The HOL4 theorem covers valid memory-mapped I/O requests. The paper appeared in the ACM PLOS workshop proceedings, classified here as a proceedings volume.
results.quote:
For the i2c_reg_top submodule, we have completed all the
three steps of Section 3.1, resulting in a proof of behavioural
equivalence between the spec and the original Verilog design.

results.finding: Hydra illustrates 1 confined Tax procedure call that can write its result to the caller’s object while blocking writes through inherited references.
results.detail: The implementation uses UCNFRTS to trigger confinement. The guarantee evaluated here covers writes through object references.
results.quote:
Just as MDFYRTS masks MDFYRTS on loads, it
masks MDFYRTS in all capabilities in the incarnated LNS
inherited from the procedure (but not those passed as
arguments).

results.finding: For one kernel, mCertiKOS-secure, Coq verifies modeled process noninterference across approximately 3,000 lines of C and the linked assembly.
results.detail: The process-local semantics collapses other processes’ execution into a single yield step. The low-level theorem compares output-buffer observations without measuring elapsed steps or modeling the x86 timestamp counter.
results.quote:
We successfully developed a fully-formalized Coq
proof that guarantees security of the low-level model of the
kernel’s assembly execution.

results.finding: In seL4’s abstract specification, Isabelle/HOL proofs established preservation of the kernel-object invariant for 2 of the 3 routines called directly by call_kernel.
results.detail: The proof assumes a well-formed post-initialisation state and an axiomatized cache-colour allocation. Thread activation also requires a valid pointer in the current domain and a thread control block at that address. The event handler remains open.
results.quote: proofs completed for them, completing two of the three functions called bycall kernel.

results.finding: RISC-V seL4 touched-address refinement was demonstrated on 2 procedures, lookupCap and updateCap, with limited proof coverage.
results.detail: The lookupCap proof assumes both correspondence and a specification lemma for resolveAddressBitsInDomPart. The updateCap correspondence for cap_untyped_cap_set_capFreeIndex remains incomplete.
results.quote:
I proved correspondence between
updateCapInDomPart and the operation*slot = cap.

results.finding: The seL4 notification implementation coalesces signals to wake at most one thread. The Cheshire benchmark protocol specifies 20,000 samples per test.
results.detail: The security argument assumes state-independent signalling, a valid worst-case bound for padding, and a timer interval long enough for notification delivery.
results.quote:
A signal will only ever unblock a single thread,

results.finding: Parfait proved circuit-to-interface refinement for all 4 hardware security module implementations.
results.detail: The end-to-end proof connects mechanized subproofs with an on-paper argument. Its scope is cycle-level digital I/O, including timing, under the stated driver and toolchain assumptions.
results.quote:
Parfait proves IPR between the application specification and
the SoC running the app and system software

results.finding: Coq proofs cover mCertiKOS drivers and interrupt handlers for all 3 modeled devices: UART, IOAPIC, and LAPIC.
results.detail: The UART proof assumes that a transmission acknowledgment arrives within 12,800 calls to delay(). The verified runtime model assumes a single processor and nonpreemptive user processes. The paper appeared in the peer-reviewed PLDI conference proceedings.
results.quote:
Using our general device interface, we
have modeled a serial device and two interrupt controller
devices. On top of these device models, we have veriﬁed the
related drivers and interrupt handlers.

results.finding: Ironclad proves app-specific information-flow guarantees for 4 standalone full-stack images.
results.detail: Verified kernel invariants and IOMMU configuration support the proof. It assumes correct CPU, memory, and chipset behavior, plus secure late launch and TPM support. Timing, cache effects, and liveness are outside the proof.
results.quote:
The proof for each
app, in turn, builds on lemmas about lower-level libraries,
drivers, and OS, which we discuss in§6.

definition = "A caller can give confidential data to an untrusted program and receive its result. The execution environment prevents the program from disclosing information to anyone the policy does not authorise. Under its stated hardware and software assumptions, the guarantee covers both storage channels, where another program can read a change in shared state, and timing channels, where another program can observe a change in how long an operation takes.". Reason: The definition leaves storage channels unexplained and treats shared hardware as a channel without identifying what another program observes.

goal.need = "A browser needs to know which sites its user visits. Of 424 Android browsers studied, 37 shared browsing history for which investigators could identify no feature requiring disclosure. Confinement would let people give third-party software the data it needs and still control who may learn it. Memory permissions alone cannot provide that control. Even programs with separate memory can communicate through changes in execution time, so the guarantee depends on hardware that lets the operating system isolate those timing effects.". Reason: The existing paragraph reports a kernel experiment without explaining whose information is at risk or why restricting access to it is insufficient.

add statement by German Cyberagentur, ÖvIT programme, PISTIs-V project description, n.d.: "Dadurch werden keine geschützten Informationen preisgegeben, auch nicht durch mikroarchitektonische Timing-Kanäle.". Reason: The funding programme explicitly names the confinement property that the existing PISTIs-V statement describes only as a general security goal.

The policy defines which releases are allowed."; threshold_quote = "Die verifizierten Eigenschaften von LionsOS beinhalten den Beweis, dass nicht vertrauensw\u00fcrdige Komponenten eingeschr\u00e4nkt werden. Reason: The programme identifies the processor mechanism and requires the driver proof to use the verified implementation of the corresponding device, two conditions left implicit in the criterion.

edit m1: title = "A machine-checked proof establishes nonleakage for a kernel's C implementation."; criterion = "Prove that each partition's observations depend only on authorised sources and the scheduler. Start from a configured kernel state satisfying the invariants, a consistent and well-formed access policy, the safety condition on cross-partition capabilities, and the timer-only interrupt restriction. The theorem covers storage channels and logical time and assumes correct compilation, assembly, hardware and boot code."; threshold_quote = "Theorem 2: seL4\u2019s C implementation enforces information flow security."; threshold_ref = 7. Reason: The criterion mixes the theorem's hypotheses with the date and size of the implementation for which it was proved.

edit m2: title = "One channel measures below 1 millibit per input or within the 95% zero-leakage bound."; criterion = "For one specified channel and configuration, estimate mutual information M in bits per input. Record M < 0.001 bit as below the tool's resolution. Otherwise shuffle the association between inputs and outputs 100 times and use the shuffled estimates to calculate M\u2080, the upper 95% bound under zero leakage. Record M \u2264 M\u2080 as consistent with zero leakage. Both conclusions apply only to the tested channel and dataset."; threshold_quote = "others are consistent with no channel or below the 1 mb tool resolution."; threshold_ref = 1. Reason: The revised criterion distinguishes a measurement below tool resolution from one consistent with zero and removes the result for a particular processor.

edit m3: title = "An OS model enforces confidentiality for every observing domain, including its observations of time."; criterion = "Machine-check observer-relative confidentiality for every user domain in a generic OS model. Include observable time, partitioned and resettable processor state, interrupts and the communication that the policy permits. Under the model's hardware and OS assumptions, each domain's observations may depend on another domain's data only through the specified policy channels."; threshold_quote = "Theorem 1 (OS model enforces confidentiality with time protection)."; threshold_ref = 9. Reason: The theorem defines the test for every observing domain, while the existing criterion also recounts the authors' particular two-system-call result.

add milestone after m3: "seL4's abstract specification bounds the addresses touched on behalf of each security domain.". Reason: Roadmap task 2A supplies the missing step between the generic OS theorem and refinement of seL4's own specification to C.

add milestone after m5: "A proof establishes that CVA6's fence.t instruction enforces its timing-isolation contract.". Reason: The existing milestones leave the kernel's processor contract as an assumption even though the programme calls for verification of the hardware that implements it.

split m4 into "A refinement proof establishes time protection for seL4's C implementation." | "Verified seL4 communication mechanisms preserve time protection across security domains.". Reason: The roadmap treats carrying time protection to the kernel implementation and preserving it across cross-domain communication as separately verifiable results.

split m5 into "A device implementation provably refines its formal interface specification." | "A device driver is proved correct against its specified hardware and OS interfaces.". Reason: Proving that hardware implements an interface and proving that a driver uses an interface correctly are distinct obligations that can be met for different devices.
